abstract: Biodiversity loss generally impairs functions on which nature and societies depend upon. Yet, it is difficult to predict under which conditions losing biodiversity has larger effects on functions such as primary production or carbon retention. We present a theory that demonstrates that biotic interactions mediate the intensity of these effects. In species interaction networks with many or strong trophic links, biodiversity loss has weaker effects on functioning because alternative interaction pathways allow surviving species to compensate for species loss. In contrast, in networks with fewer or weaker links, ecosystem functioning is very sensitive to the extinction of species. Here, we identify interaction erosion as a hidden dimension of the biodiversity crisis that provides a unifying explanation for functional consequences of biodiversity loss across ecological contexts.
